answer.sourceLine: Confirmed word for word in Keller’s own journal: the entry headed “The Manse, December 10th” — written at the manse in Bothwell, Scotland — on page 57 of Helen Keller’s Journal, 1936–1937 (Doubleday, Doran & Company, 1938). She set it down on the day Edward VIII signed the Instrument of Abdication, as her reason for doubting he would find the happiness he expected.

source.excerpt: Many persons have a wrong idea of what constitutes true happiness. It is not attained through self-gratification but through fidelity to a worthy purpose. Happiness should be a means of accomplishment, like health, not an end in itself.
trail: 1936 — written. Anne Sullivan Macy died on October 20, 1936; Keller and Polly Thomson sailed for Scotland, and Keller began the journal aboard the SS Deutschland at midnight on November 4, 1936. By December 10th she was at the manse in Bothwell, where she wrote the entry containing this sentence (full text ↗).

The same day, in London. The entry records that King Edward VIII has abdicated, and the sentence is Keller’s stated reason for doubting he will find the happiness he expects. The Royal Family dates the signing of the Instrument of Abdication to 10 December 1936, effective the next day (royal.uk ↗).

1938 — first published. Doubleday, Doran & Company issued the journal in Garden City, New York, with the notice “Copyright, 1938, by Helen Keller — all rights reserved” and a foreword by Nella Braddy. The passage falls between the printed markers for pages 56 and 57 in the scanned first edition (Internet Archive ↗).

Confirmed by the specialists. Wikiquote lists the line among Keller’s sourced quotations, citing Helen Keller’s Journal: 1936–1937 (1938), p. 57 (Wikiquote ↗), and Quote Investigator concludes Keller crafted the quotation and placed it into her journal in 1936, listing reprints from a 1950 anthology onward (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.excerptNote: The paragraph is not about self-improvement. Keller has just written that Edward VIII has abdicated and that she doubts he will reap the happiness he anticipates; she then argues that happiness is a by-product of duty, and closes by insisting that no one has a right to consume happiness without producing it. These sentences are reproduced from page 57 of the 1938 first edition for identification and provenance only — the book is still in copyright.

source.rightsNote: The sentence was first published in Helen Keller’s Journal, 1936–1937 (1938), which carries the notice “Copyright, 1938, by Helen Keller — all rights reserved.” A book first published in 1938 is not in the United States public domain in 2026, so this passage is quoted here briefly for identification and provenance rather than reproduced at length. Keller’s much earlier books — The Story of My Life (1903), The World I Live In (1910), Midstream (1929) — stand on different footing, but this line is not from any of them.

author.name: Helen Keller

author.metaLine: 1880–1968 · American author, lecturer and advocate for the blind
author.bio: Helen Keller was deaf and blind from early childhood; Anne Sullivan arrived in Tuscumbia, Alabama on March 3, 1887 to begin her education and stayed with her, as “Teacher,” for nearly half a century. Keller thought of herself as a writer first — the American Foundation for the Blind notes that her passport listed her profession as “author” — and she worked with the Foundation for more than forty years. This sentence comes from the journal she kept in the months immediately after Sullivan’s death, which her editor described as a record of her awakening from a great spiritual numbness.

misattribution.heading: The author is right — the wording and the source are what go wrong
misattribution.intro: This is one of the rare famous-name quotations that survives scrutiny: Keller really wrote it. What travels badly is everything around it. Quote sites reprint it with a swapped article, chop it into a slogan, or print it with no source at all — which is exactly why it reads like an invented inspirational line.

items.why: The Quotations Page carries this variant with no source document or publication reference of any kind (quotationspage.com ↗). The journal reads “a wrong idea.”

items.who: “Happiness is attained through fidelity to a worthy purpose.”
items.why: Quotefancy prints this eight-word remnant with no publication cited (quotefancy.com ↗). It discards the contrast — not through self-gratification but through fidelity — that is the whole point of Keller’s sentence. An ellipsis-spliced “True happiness… is not attained through self-gratification…” form circulates just as widely.

Goodreads carries the correct wording but no book, page or date, and states outright that its quotes are added by the community and are not verified (goodreads.com ↗). A real, checkable citation exists — it simply is not the one being copied.

Shared as a free-floating maxim about personal fulfilment. In the journal it is a moral judgment on a specific public event — Edward VIII giving up the throne — and it sits beside Keller’s much harder claim that no one has a right to consume happiness without producing it.

misattribution.truthLine: Attribution: correct. Provenance: Helen Keller’s journal entry of December 10, 1936, page 57 of Helen Keller’s Journal, 1936–1937 (Doubleday, Doran & Company, 1938) — readable in the scanned first edition (Internet Archive ↗) and cited to the same page by Wikiquote ↗.

context.heading: Written on the day a king gave up his throne
lead: This is not a self-help maxim. Anne Sullivan Macy — the “Teacher” of Keller’s entire life — died on October 20, 1936. Keller sailed for Scotland with her companion Polly Thomson and began this journal aboard the SS Deutschland at midnight on November 4, 1936; the editor’s foreword calls the book a record of her awakening from a great spiritual numbness into a renewed determination to make her life of service to others (full text ↗).

The December 10th entry opens with the news reaching Bothwell from London: Edward VIII had abdicated. Keller wrote that she doubted His Majesty would reap from his decision the happiness he anticipated — and the famous sentence is the reasoning she offers for that doubt. The Royal Family dates the signing of the Instrument of Abdication to 10 December 1936, with the Abdication Act taking effect the following day (royal.uk ↗).
detailsBody: The Internet Archive holds a scan of the Doubleday, Doran first edition, which carries the notice “Copyright, 1938, by Helen Keller — all rights reserved” and a foreword by Nella Braddy. Searching its OCR text returns the sentence intact inside the December 10th entry, and the printed page markers place it on page 57 (scanned edition ↗).

Two independent authorities agree on the same location: Wikiquote lists the line in its sourced section citing Helen Keller’s Journal: 1936–1937 (1938), p. 57, and Quote Investigator traces it to the December 10, 1936 entry, listing later reprints from a 1950 anthology onward (Quote Investigator ↗).

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator traces the quotation to Helen Keller's journal entry of December 10, 1936, published in Helen Keller's Journal 1936-1937 (Doubleday, Doran, 1938), concludes Keller crafted it herself, and lists later reprints beginning with a 1950 anthology.
Wikiquote lists the quotation in its sourced section for Helen Keller (not Misattributed or Disputed), citing Helen Keller's Journal: 1936-1937 (1938), p. 57.

The full OCR text of the 1938 first edition contains the sentence verbatim inside the entry headed 'The Manse, December 10th', between the printed page markers [56] and [57]; the same entry records that Edward VIII has abdicated and that Keller doubts he will reap the happiness he anticipates. Front matter shows 'Copyright, 1938, by Helen Keller / All rights reserved', 'Doubleday, Doran & Company, Inc., Garden City, New York', 'First edition'; Nella Braddy's foreword states Anne Sullivan Macy died October 20, 1936 and that Keller began the journal aboard the SS Deutschland at midnight of November 4, 1936. Earlier entry headers read 'The Manse, Bothwell'.

The Internet Archive item is Helen Keller's Journal, 1936-1937 by Helen Keller, published 1938 by Doubleday, Doran and Company, Inc., 330 pages, available to download and borrow, described as a record of her awakening from a great spiritual numbness into a renewed determination to make her life service to others.

The American Foundation for the Blind biography gives Helen Adams Keller's dates as June 27, 1880 to June 1, 1968, notes she saw herself as a writer first with her passport listing her profession as 'author', and records over 40 years of work with the American Foundation for the Blind.

The Royal Family's page states Edward VIII signed the Instrument of Abdication on 10 December 1936, and that it became effective the following day, 11 December 1936, when he gave Royal Assent to His Majesty's Declaration of Abdication Act.

Wikipedia confirms Helen Keller was born June 27, 1880 and died June 1, 1968, lists 'Helen Keller's journal (1938)' among her works, and states Anne Sullivan Macy died on October 20, 1936 with Keller holding her hand.

The Quotations Page prints the variant wording 'Many persons have the wrong idea of what constitutes true happiness. It is not attained through self-gratification but through fidelity to a worthy purpose.' attributed to Helen Keller with no original source document or publication reference.
Quotefancy prints the truncated form 'Happiness is attained through fidelity to a worthy purpose.' attributed to Helen Keller with no book, speech, or other source cited.
Goodreads carries the full correct wording attributed to Helen Keller with no book or source cited, and notes that quotes are added by the Goodreads community and are not verified by Goodreads.
